name: Tiber Green
lede: Tiber Green is a pale yellow-green named, by our library's own classification, for the Tiber, and its single strongest match in our painting archive is Vincent van Gogh's *Roses*, where it covers nearly half the canvas.

sections.title: A river's name on a 1912 plate
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* records this hue at plate XVIII, hue 33′, tone d, and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary repeats it at plate 18, position E 6, dated to the same year [1]. The ISCC-NBS system later filed it as a light yellow-green [1]. Our color library classes it as a place-or-institution name, built on "Tiber" [2]. Beyond that classification, nothing in our sources confirms whether the name points to the river that runs through Rome or to some other use of the word [2].

Its closest named relative is [[light-grey-green]], just 3.1 units away and almost indistinguishable, followed by [[veronese-green]], a touch yellower [3].

Further out are [[greenish-hospital-green]] and [[greenish-hospital-green]], both greener at 4.6 units [3]. Our library files the color under fashion and textiles rather than nature, which is worth noting for a name that otherwise reads as a landscape color [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Tiber Green is uncommon in our archive of 23,781 paintings: a color within six units of it covers at least five per cent of a canvas in only 14 works, as photographed [4]. The strongest of them is Van Gogh's 1890 *Roses*, where it covers 44 per cent of the canvas, a painting whose colors read very differently today than the pinks its title promises [4]. Across its matches overall, 93 per cent of the coverage sits in highlights rather than mid-tones or shadow [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so every figure is a screen color, not a pigment identification [4]. Mughal painting carries the color at about ten times the archive's overall rate, and works from Russia and the United States carry it at several times the rate too [4].
